claim: Grid cells in the entorhinal cortex allow for the precise decoding of position in space.
source: Grid cells in the entorhinal cortex allow for the precise decoding of position in space.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about grid cells.

claim: Grid cells have been hypothesized to make a general contribution to mental operations.
source: Along with potentially playing an important role in navigation, grid cells have recently been hypothesized to make a general contribution to mental operations.
evidence: This references a hypothesis in the literature without specific citation in this sentence.

claim: Movement of covert attention, without any physical movement, elicits spatial receptive fields with a triangular tiling of space.
source: Here, we show that movement of covert attention, without any physical movement, also elicits spatial receptive fields with a triangular tiling of space.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 20 out of 141 entorhinal cells (14%) showed spatially structured receptive fields at FDR <5%.
source: In monkeys trained to maintain central fixation while covertly attending to a stimulus moving in the periphery we identified a significant population (20/141, 14% neurons at a FDR <5%) of entorhinal cells with spatially structured receptive fields.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Grid-like representations were not observed in hippocampal recordings during the covert attention task.
source: This contrasts with recordings obtained in the hippocampus, where grid-like representations were not observed.
evidence: This is a negative finding from control recordings in the hippocampus.

claim: Neurons in macaque entorhinal cortex do not rely on physical movement.
source: Our results provide evidence that neurons in macaque entorhinal cortex do not rely on physical movement.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Spatial representations in the form of place cells and grid cells have been identified in rodents.
source: Spatial representations, in the form of place cells and grid cells, have been identified in rodents (Hafting et al., 2005; O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), bats (Yartsev et al., 2011; Yartsev and Ulanovsky, 2013), macaque monkeys (Killian et al., 2012) and humans (Jacobs et al., 2013; Ekstrom et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Spatial representations in the form of place cells and grid cells have been identified in bats.
source: Spatial representations, in the form of place cells and grid cells, have been identified in rodents (Hafting et al., 2005; O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), bats (Yartsev et al., 2011; Yartsev and Ulanovsky, 2013), macaque monkeys (Killian et al., 2012) and humans (Jacobs et al., 2013; Ekstrom et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Spatial representations in the form of place cells and grid cells have been identified in macaque monkeys.
source: Spatial representations, in the form of place cells and grid cells, have been identified in rodents (Hafting et al., 2005; O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), bats (Yartsev et al., 2011; Yartsev and Ulanovsky, 2013), macaque monkeys (Killian et al., 2012) and humans (Jacobs et al., 2013; Ekstrom et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Spatial representations in the form of place cells and grid cells have been identified in humans.
source: Spatial representations, in the form of place cells and grid cells, have been identified in rodents (Hafting et al., 2005; O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), bats (Yartsev et al., 2011; Yartsev and Ulanovsky, 2013), macaque monkeys (Killian et al., 2012) and humans (Jacobs et al., 2013; Ekstrom et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The hippocampal formation contributes to the processing of memories.
source: The hippocampal formation, however, also contributes to the processing of memories (Squire and Wixted, 2011), and conceptual similarities between spatial navigation and the processes involved in remembering and planning suggest that grid cells might support cognitive functions besides spatial navigation (Buzsáki et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Conceptual similarities between spatial navigation and the processes involved in remembering and planning suggest that grid cells might support cognitive functions besides spatial navigation.
source: The hippocampal formation, however, also contributes to the processing of memories (Squire and Wixted, 2011), and conceptual similarities between spatial navigation and the processes involved in remembering and planning suggest that grid cells might support cognitive functions besides spatial navigation (Buzsáki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: Grid cells are active during the exploration of images with eye-movements (overt attention).
source: This idea resonates well with the recent demonstration that grid cells are active during the exploration of images with eye-movements, that is by overt attention (Killian et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Grid cells do not only track an animal's location in space, but can also represent the gaze position of the animal.
source: These findings revealed that grid cells do not only track an animal's location in space, but can also represent the gaze position of the animal.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings of Killian et al., 2012, referenced in the previous sentence.

claim: Shifts of gaze location usually correspond to shifts in attention.
source: Shifts of gaze location usually correspond to shifts in attention (Hoffman, 1998; Rolfs et al., 2011), and the neural substrate for overt and covert attention is largely overlapping (Corbetta et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The neural substrate for overt and covert attention is largely overlapping.
source: Shifts of gaze location usually correspond to shifts in attention (Hoffman, 1998; Rolfs et al., 2011), and the neural substrate for overt and covert attention is largely overlapping (Corbetta et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Grid cells in the entorhinal cortex are potentially capable of representing the locus of attention in general.
source: Accordingly, grid cells in the entorhinal cortex are potentially capable of representing not only gaze location but the locus of attention in general.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the overlap between overt and covert attention systems.

claim: Attention functions as an important control for mental processes.
source: Attention functions as an important control for mental processes (Petersen and Posner, 2012); accordingly, the hypothesis that grid cells participate in a range of cognitive functions predicts that grid cells may be activated by movements of attention.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The hypothesis that grid cells participate in a range of cognitive functions predicts that grid cells may be activated by movements of attention.
source: Attention functions as an important control for mental processes (Petersen and Posner, 2012); accordingly, the hypothesis that grid cells participate in a range of cognitive functions predicts that grid cells may be activated by movements of attention.
evidence: This is a logical prediction derived from the hypothesis about grid cell function.

claim: 141 neurons were recorded in the entorhinal cortex of two rhesus macaque monkeys performing a covert attention tracking task.
source: To examine spatial representations of cells in the entorhinal cortex during the movement of covert attention, we recorded the neuronal activity of 141 neurons in the entorhinal cortex of two rhesus macaque monkeys performing a covert attention tracking task.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size.

claim: Monkeys were trained to maintain central fixation while attending to a small (1°) dot that moved around the computer monitor.
source: The monkeys were trained to maintain central fixation while attending to a small (1°) dot that moved around the computer monitor (see Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental task design, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The task required monkeys to respond by quickly releasing a response bar when the dot changed color.
source: The task of the monkey was to respond by quickly releasing a response bar when the dot changed color.
evidence: This describes the behavioral task requirement.

claim: The color change occurred after a random time interval (700 – 2000 ms) following trial onset.
source: The color change occurred after a random time interval (700 – 2000 ms) following trial onset.
evidence: This describes a specific parameter of the experimental design.

claim: The dot traced out several Hamiltonian cycles, ensuring that each screen location was visited equally often.
source: Over the course of a recording session, the dot traced out several Hamiltonian cycles, thereby ensuring that in the limit of infinitely many cycles each screen location was visited equally often.
evidence: This describes the trajectory design to ensure uniform spatial sampling.

claim: Monkeys performed the task at >70% accuracy, with the majority of errors due to saccades outside of the fixation window.
source: Monkeys performed the task at >70% accuracy, with the majority of errors due to saccades to outside of the fixation window.
evidence: This reports behavioral performance data.

claim: Monkeys completed between two and eight cycles per session depending on their motivation.
source: Depending on their motivation, monkeys completed between two and eight cycles per session.
evidence: This reports the range of data collection per session.

claim: Grid cells possess a regular firing field with increased firing rates at the nodes of equilateral triangles that evenly tile space.
source: Grid cells possess a regular firing field with increased firing rates at the nodes of equilateral triangles that evenly tile space.
evidence: This is a definition of grid cells based on established knowledge.

claim: Tiling space with equilateral triangles leads to 2D autocorrelation functions with six peaks arranged in a hexagonal structure around the center peak.
source: Importantly, tiling space with equilateral triangles leads to 2D autocorrelation functions with six peaks arranged in a hexagonal structure around the center peak.
evidence: This describes a mathematical property of grid cell firing patterns.

claim: The gridness score normalizes away the absolute firing rate modulation over space.
source: An important property of the gridness score is that the autocorrelation normalizes away the absolute firing rate modulation over space.
evidence: This describes a property of the gridness measure used in the analysis.

claim: The gridness score is susceptible to noise, and homogeneous firing fields might produce high gridness scores by chance.
source: The gridness score is therefore susceptible to noise, and homogeneous firing fields might produce high gridness scores by chance.
evidence: This is a limitation of the gridness measure acknowledged by the authors.

claim: A firing field modulation index was computed to better differentiate between noisy and grid-like firing fields.
source: To better differentiate between noisy and grid-like firing fields, we computed for each cell an index of firing field modulation from its estimated rate map and a gridness score from its 2D autocorrelation function (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes a methodological innovation introduced in this study.

claim: Cells were simulated by creating spike-trains with an inhomogeneous Poisson process.
source: Cells were simulated by creating spike-trains with an inhomogeneous Poisson (IP) process (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the simulation method used for statistical validation.

claim: Simulated cells with a homogeneous firing field control for any potential grid-like structure in the dot's trajectory.
source: Simulated cells with a homogeneous firing field therefore control for any potential grid-like structure in the dot's trajectory.
evidence: This explains the purpose of the control simulations.

claim: A log likelihood ratio was computed to differentiate grid cells from place cells and homogeneous cells.
source: To differentiate grid cells, we computed the log likelihood ratio for comparing grid cells with place cells and homogeneous cells (Figure 3 and Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the statistical method used for cell classification.

claim: A threshold of 4.25 deciban corresponds to a false discovery rate <5%.
source: Out of 141 recorded neurons, we identified 20 cells (14%) with a log likelihood ratio of >4.25 deciban (corresponding to a false discovery rate <5%) in favor of cells with spatially structured firing fields according to the two criteria of modulation index and gridness score.
evidence: This reports the statistical threshold and corresponding FDR from simulations.

claim: Cells classified as grid cells had a lower mean firing rate (0.47 Hz) compared to those classified as other cells (1.22 Hz).
source: Cells classified as grid cells had a lower mean firing rate (0.47 Hz) compared to those classified as other cells (1.22 Hz), and higher average gridness (1.29 vs. 0.51) and firing field modulation index values (0.1 vs. 0.04).
evidence: This reports quantitative differences between classified cell types.

claim: Cells classified as grid cells had higher average gridness (1.29 vs. 0.51) compared to other cells.
source: Cells classified as grid cells had a lower mean firing rate (0.47 Hz) compared to those classified as other cells (1.22 Hz), and higher average gridness (1.29 vs. 0.51) and firing field modulation index values (0.1 vs. 0.04).
evidence: This reports quantitative differences between classified cell types.

claim: Cells classified as grid cells had higher firing field modulation index values (0.1 vs. 0.04) compared to other cells.
source: Cells classified as grid cells had a lower mean firing rate (0.47 Hz) compared to those classified as other cells (1.22 Hz), and higher average gridness (1.29 vs. 0.51) and firing field modulation index values (0.1 vs. 0.04).
evidence: This reports quantitative differences between classified cell types.

claim: More conservative thresholds of 10 and 20 deciban correspond to false discovery rates of 1.26% and 0.07%, respectively.
source: We also tested more conservative thresholds of 10 and 20 deciban (false discovery rates of 1.26% and 0.07%, respectively), which require more evidence to classify a cell as a grid cell.
evidence: This reports additional statistical thresholds tested.

claim: A population of neurons was labeled as grid cells on an individual basis with high significance (X2(1, N = 141, FDR = 0.05) = 25.0, p < 0.0001).
source: Regardless of the threshold used, we were able to identify a population of neurons that were labeled as grid cells on an individual basis with high significance (X2(1, N = 141, FDR = 0.05) = 25.0, p < 0.0001, 20, 9 and 3 cells w.r.t. to false discovery rates for different thresholds).
evidence: This reports the statistical significance of the grid cell population.

claim: 307 neurons were recorded from the hippocampus in monkeys performing the same task.
source: First we recorded neuronal activity of 307 neurons from the hippocampus in monkeys performing the same task.
evidence: This describes a control experiment.

claim: There are currently no reports of grid cells in the hippocampus.
source: There are currently no reports of grid cells in the hippocampus and these neurons can therefore serve as a baseline to determine our empirical false discovery rate.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the literature.

claim: Classifying hippocampal cells with the same measures and the 5% FDR threshold yielded an empirical false-discovery rate of 8.5%.
source: Classifying these cells with the same measures and the 5% FDR threshold yielded an empirical false-discovery rate of 8.5%.
evidence: This reports the empirical FDR from the hippocampal control data.

claim: The hippocampal recordings likely contain a different ratio of spatially structured (e.g. place cells) to spatial noise cells.
source: The FDR is slightly higher than the FDR derived from simulations because the hippocampal recordings likely contain a different ratio of spatially structured (e.g. place cells) to spatial noise cells.
evidence: This is an explanation for the difference between simulated and empirical FDR.

claim: In the entorhinal cortex, significantly more grid-cells were found than expected from a FDR of 8.5% (X2(1, N = 141, FDR = 0.085) = 5.9, p = 0.016).
source: Yet, in the entorhinal cortex (see above), we find significantly more grid-cells than expected from a FDR of 8.5% (X2(1, N = 141, FDR = 0.085) = 5.9, p = 0.016; p < 0.05 for classifying with the 10 and 20 deciban thresholds as well).
evidence: This reports statistical comparison with the empirical FDR.

claim: A bootstrapping analysis was used to create a joint distribution of indices when the association between firing rate and the dot's position is destroyed.
source: Second, we used a bootstrapping analysis to create a joint distribution of indices when the association between firing rate and the dot's position is destroyed.
evidence: This describes an additional control analysis method.

claim: The bootstrapping analysis found an empirical false discovery rate of 5.5%.
source: We again computed both indices and found an empirical false discovery rate of 5.5%.
evidence: This reports the result of the bootstrapping control analysis.

claim: Combining spikes generated by different firing fields destroys the spatial structure of the individual firing fields.
source: First, combining spikes generated by different firing fields destroys the spatial structure of the individual firing fields.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the effect of pooling neurons.

claim: None of the pooled units (all neurons in each recording session) was classified as having a grid-like firing field.
source: We therefore pooled all neurons in each recording session and calculated gridness scores and firing field modulation indices. None of these pooled units was classified as having a grid-like firing field (average and max gridness score 0.36/0.96, average and max firing field modulation 0.02/0.11).
evidence: This reports the result of a control analysis pooling neurons.

claim: None of the trajectory-only units (pooled trajectories with equal firing rate at all locations) was classified as a grid cell.
source: For each recording session, we pooled all trajectories and computed gridness scores and firing field modulation indices by assuming an equal firing rate at all locations. None of these units was classified as a grid cell (average and max gridness score 0.1/1.17, average and max firing field modulation 0.018/0.033).
evidence: This reports the result of a control analysis examining trajectory structure.

claim: The results are not due to an inherent grid-like structure in the trajectories.
source: These controls demonstrate that our results are not due to an inherent grid-like structure in the trajectories.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control analyses.

claim: No substantial correlations were found between eye-position and dot position.
source: However, we found no substantial correlations between eye-position and dot position.
evidence: This reports the result of an analysis examining potential eye-tracking confounds.

claim: Average correlations between eye-position and dot position within a session were small (mean = −0.005).
source: Average correlations within a session were small (mean = −0.005) and within the expected range of correlations when we shuffled trials in time and thereby assigning eye-movement positions to dot trajectories from different parts within a session (mean 0.001, 5 and 95% percentile: −0.02, 0.02).
evidence: This reports quantitative results of the eye-tracking analysis.

claim: The monkeys did not track the dot with small eye movements.
source: We conclude that the monkeys did not track the dot with small eye movements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the eye-tracking analysis.

claim: Cells classified as grid cells in both animals showed, on average, increased firing rates on the contralateral side of the visual field relative to the recorded hemisphere.
source: While cells classified as grid cells (5% FDR) in both animals showed, on average, increased firing rates on the contralateral side of the visual field relative to the recorded hemisphere, these differences were not consistent across cells (mean contralateral-ipsilateral = 0.06, t = −1.99, p = 0.06, one sample t-test).
evidence: This reports an analysis of potential hemispheric biases in firing rates.

claim: No difference in firing rate was found between the central five degrees of visual field and the rest of the visual field.
source: Second, we computed an index that compares average firing rate within the central five degrees of visual field around the fixation cross with the rest of the visual field. We again found no difference in firing rate (mean center-periphery = 0.08, t = 1.7, p = 0.10).
evidence: This reports an analysis of potential eccentricity biases in firing rates.

claim: The experimental conditions are most sensitive for firing fields with a size that allows multiple repetitions of the grid on the screen.
source: An important caveat is that our experimental conditions are most sensitive for firing fields with a size that allows multiple repetitions of the grid on the screen.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: Larger firing fields might appear like place or homogeneous cells.
source: Larger firing fields might appear like place or homogeneous cells, and firing fields with spacing smaller than the spacing of our trajectories will appear as spatially structured noise.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of the detection method.

claim: The results likely represent a conservative estimate of the percentage of grid cells in the entorhinal cortex.
source: We can therefore make no definitive statements about the percentage of grid cells in the entorhinal cortex, and our results likely represent a conservative estimate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the limitations of the study.

claim: The activation of cells in entorhinal cortex with spatially structured firing fields does not require physical movement through an environment.
source: In summary, our results provide strong evidence that the activation of cells in entorhinal cortex with spatially structured firing fields does not require physical movement through an environment.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Grid cells can be activated by eye movements as monkeys visually explore complex scenes.
source: Previous results demonstrated that, in stationary monkeys, grid cells can be activated by eye movements as monkeys visually explore complex scenes (Killian et al., 2012).
evidence: This references a prior finding from the literature.

claim: Even eye movements are not required to activate cells with grid-like firing fields.
source: Here, our findings suggest that even eye movements are not required to activate cells with grid-like firing fields and that firing fields in the entorhinal cortex cells can represent the location of attention.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings.

claim: Firing fields in the entorhinal cortex cells can represent the location of attention.
source: Here, our findings suggest that even eye movements are not required to activate cells with grid-like firing fields and that firing fields in the entorhinal cortex cells can represent the location of attention.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings.

claim: Theta phase precession has been identified in rodents.
source: That spatial representations in the hippocampal formation can represent locations other than the animal's current position has been shown in rodents through the identification of theta phase precession (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993) and the demonstration that ensembles of hippocampal place cells fire in sequence within a theta cycle, representing places in front of and behind the animal (Muller and Kubie, 1989; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Jensen and Lisman, 1996).
evidence: This references prior findings from the literature.

claim: Ensembles of hippocampal place cells fire in sequence within a theta cycle, representing places in front of and behind the animal.
source: That spatial representations in the hippocampal formation can represent locations other than the animal's current position has been shown in rodents through the identification of theta phase precession (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993) and the demonstration that ensembles of hippocampal place cells fire in sequence within a theta cycle, representing places in front of and behind the animal (Muller and Kubie, 1989; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Jensen and Lisman, 1996).
evidence: This references prior findings from the literature.

claim: Sequential firing of hippocampal place cells can represent anticipation of upcoming locations.
source: More recent studies have shown that sequential firing of hippocampal place cells can represent anticipation of upcoming locations (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007), future possible paths when the rat is at a choice point (Johnson and Redish, 2007; Singer et al., 2013), and even behavioral trajectories toward a remembered goal in a 2D environment (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013).
evidence: This references prior findings from the literature.

claim: Sequential firing of hippocampal place cells can represent future possible paths when the rat is at a choice point.
source: More recent studies have shown that sequential firing of hippocampal place cells can represent anticipation of upcoming locations (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007), future possible paths when the rat is at a choice point (Johnson and Redish, 2007; Singer et al., 2013), and even behavioral trajectories toward a remembered goal in a 2D environment (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013).
evidence: This references prior findings from the literature.

claim: Sequential firing of hippocampal place cells can represent behavioral trajectories toward a remembered goal in a 2D environment.
source: More recent studies have shown that sequential firing of hippocampal place cells can represent anticipation of upcoming locations (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007), future possible paths when the rat is at a choice point (Johnson and Redish, 2007; Singer et al., 2013), and even behavioral trajectories toward a remembered goal in a 2D environment (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013).
evidence: This references prior findings from the literature.

claim: Hippocampal sequences may reflect the animal's attention being directed along a specific spatial trajectory.
source: While it is difficult in rodents to assess the location of attention distinct from the location of the animal, these data are consistent with the idea that hippocampal sequences may reflect the animal's attention being directed along a specific spatial trajectory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior findings in the context of attention.

claim: Paying attention to the just-completed trajectory could serve to enhance encoding of that experience.
source: Paying attention to the just-completed trajectory could serve to enhance encoding of that experience.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the function of attention-directed sequences.

claim: Directing attention to future possible paths could serve as a retrieval mechanism to enable optimal choice behavior.
source: Correspondingly, directing attention to future possible paths could serve as a retrieval mechanism to enable optimal choice behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the function of attention-directed sequences.

claim: Grid-like six-fold symmetric BOLD activity occurs while participants imagine navigating in a familiar environment.
source: These findings also resonate well with reports of grid-like six-fold symmetric BOLD activity while participants imagine navigating in a familiar environment (Horner et al., 2016), imagine directions between locations in a large-scale virtual city (Bellmund et al., 2016), and navigate a purely abstract concept space (Constantinescu et al., 2016).
evidence: This references prior findings from human neuroimaging studies.

claim: Grid-like six-fold symmetric BOLD activity occurs while participants imagine directions between locations in a large-scale virtual city.
source: These findings also resonate well with reports of grid-like six-fold symmetric BOLD activity while participants imagine navigating in a familiar environment (Horner et al., 2016), imagine directions between locations in a large-scale virtual city (Bellmund et al., 2016), and navigate a purely abstract concept space (Constantinescu et al., 2016).
evidence: This references prior findings from human neuroimaging studies.

claim: Grid-like six-fold symmetric BOLD activity occurs while participants navigate a purely abstract concept space.
source: These findings also resonate well with reports of grid-like six-fold symmetric BOLD activity while participants imagine navigating in a familiar environment (Horner et al., 2016), imagine directions between locations in a large-scale virtual city (Bellmund et al., 2016), and navigate a purely abstract concept space (Constantinescu et al., 2016).
evidence: This references prior findings from human neuroimaging studies.

claim: Entorhinal cells with grid-like firing fields can encode information apart from the animal's current location.
source: The data presented here demonstrate that entorhinal cells with grid-like firing fields can similarly encode information apart from the animal's current location.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings.

claim: The percentage of grid cells found (14%) is lower than reports from recording in rats (e.g. 32% in Sargolini et al., 2006).
source: In agreement with Killian et al. (2012), we found a percentage of grid cells (14%) that is lower than reports from recording in rats (e.g. 32% in Sargolini et al., 2006).
evidence: This compares the current findings with prior literature.

claim: The task design is limited to detecting a subset of grid cells whose firing fields match the size of the screen and the spacing of the dot's trajectory.
source: First, our task design is limited to detecting a subset of grid cells who's firing fields match the size of the screen and the spacing of the dot's trajectory, thereby potentially underestimating the true percentage of grid cells in macaque entorhinal cortex.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: The task design does not attach significance to the spatial position of the dot.
source: Second, our task design does not attach significance to the spatial position of the dot.
evidence: This describes a feature of the task design.

claim: It is possible to solve the task without knowing where the color change occurs.
source: It is possible to solve the task without knowing where the color change occurs.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the task requirements.

claim: The observations may reflect the entorhinal cortex in an attenuated state.
source: Thus, it seems plausible that our observations reflect the entorhinal cortex in an attenuated state and that we would observe stronger grid cell activity if the precise dot position was relevant.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Each recording session consisted of the presentation of several cycles of the moving dot.
source: Each recording session consisted of the presentation of several cycles of the moving dot.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Cycles were smoothed Hamiltonian cycles through a 23 × 23 grid with 1° spacing and showed no center bias.
source: Cycles were smoothed Hamiltonian cycles through a 23 × 23 grid with 1°spacing and therefore showed no center bias.
evidence: This describes the trajectory design.

claim: Each cycle consisted of an average of 114 trials and took the monkeys an average of 13 min to complete.
source: Each cycle consisted of an average of 114 trials and took the monkeys an average of 13 min to complete.
evidence: This reports quantitative details of the experimental sessions.

claim: The average speed of a typical trajectory was 1.95°/s, with a maximum of 3.75°/s.
source: The average speed of a typical trajectory was 1.95°/s, with a maximum of 3.75°/s.
evidence: This reports quantitative details of the stimulus.

claim: Excluding fixation errors, monkeys performed the task at 85% accuracy across all sessions.
source: Excluding fixation errors monkeys performed the task at 85% accuracy across all sessions (min = 70%, max = 94%, std = 8%) and 87% accuracy across cycles (std = 13%).
evidence: This reports behavioral performance data.

claim: Only data from trials with correct detection of the color change and constant fixation within the fixation window were analyzed.
source: We only analyzed data from trials with correct detection of the color change and constant fixation within the fixation window.
evidence: This describes the data inclusion criteria.

claim: The monkeys were head-fixed and seated in a chair such that the monitor's center corresponded to their neutral eye position.
source: The monkeys were head-fixed and seated in a chair such that the monitor's center corresponded to their neutral eye position.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: Spikes were recorded at 40 kHz from the entorhinal cortex with a laminar electrode array mounted on a tungsten microelectrode.
source: Spikes were recorded (40 kHz) from the entorhinal cortex with a laminar electrode array mounted on a tungsten microelectrode (12-site, 150-μmm spacing; FHC).
evidence: This describes the recording methodology.

claim: Rate maps were computed with a standard Gaussian smoothing procedure.
source: Rate maps were computed with a standard Gaussian smoothing procedure (Killian et al., 2012; Brandon et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the data analysis method with citations to prior work.

claim: Gridness scores were calculated using standard equations.
source: Gridness scores were calculated using standard equations (5,14–16), but we additionally validated that our implementation was highly accurate in distinguishing grid from non-grid cells in simulated data (see 'Gridness score implementation', 'Unit simulation', 'Log likelihood ratios and classification of units' and methods Figures 2,4,5).
evidence: This describes the analysis method and validation.

claim: All experiments were carried out in accordance with protocols approved by the Emory University and University of Washington Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees.
source: All experiments were carried out in accordance with protocols approved by the Emory University and University of Washington Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: 69 units from monkey MP (seven sessions) and 72 units from monkey PW (eight sessions) were analyzed.
source: In total, we analyzed 69 units from monkey MP (seven sessions) and 72 units from monkey PW (eight sessions).
evidence: This reports the sample size for each subject.

claim: Recordings from monkey MP were carried out in the right hemisphere.
source: Recordings from monkey MP (male) were carried out in the right hemisphere and recordings from monkey PW (female) were in the left hemisphere.
evidence: This describes the recording locations for each subject.

claim: Recordings from monkey PW were carried out in the left hemisphere.
source: Recordings from monkey MP (male) were carried out in the right hemisphere and recordings from monkey PW (female) were in the left hemisphere.
evidence: This describes the recording locations for each subject.

claim: Recording sites were located in the posterior part of the entorhinal cortex and close to the rhinal sulcus.
source: Recording sites were located in the posterior part of the entorhinal cortex and close to the rhinal sulcus.
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of recordings.

claim: Units that did not show stable firing behavior through an entire cycle were discarded.
source: We discarded units that did not show stable firing behavior through an entire cycle.
evidence: This describes a data exclusion criterion.

claim: Hippocampal neurons were recorded from CA1-CA4 subfields, dentate gyrus, and subiculum.
source: Neurons were recorded from CA1-CA4 subfields, dentate gyrus, and subiculum.
evidence: This describes the anatomical locations of hippocampal recordings.

claim: For the hippocampal recordings, two to six cycles per session were recorded from the covert attention task following a ~ 1 hr recording during which monkeys freely viewed images.
source: For the hippocampal recordings, we recorded from the covert attention task for two to six cycles per session following a ~ 1 hr recording during which monkeys freely viewed images.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for hippocampal recordings.

claim: 2D histograms of spike and dot positions were computed with bins of size 0.5° × 0.5°.
source: We computed 2D histograms of spike and dot positions with bins of size 0.5° × 0.5°.
evidence: This describes a data analysis parameter.

claim: To estimate a firing rate map, both histograms were smoothed with a Gaussian kernel (σ = 1.25°) and the spike counts were divided by the amount of time the dot spent in the respective locations.
source: To estimate a firing rate map, we smoothed both histograms with a Gaussian kernel (σ = 1.25°) and divided the spike counts by the amount of time the dot spent in the respective locations.
evidence: This describes the method for computing firing rate maps.

claim: 2D autocorrelations were computed by shifting the firing rate map relative to itself and computing the coefficient of correlation for the overlapping maps.
source: 2D autocorrelations were computed by shifting the firing rate map relative to itself and computing the coefficient of correlation for the overlapping maps.
evidence: This describes the method for computing autocorrelations.

claim: The goal was to classify the reconstructed firing fields of recorded units as grid-like or not grid-like.
source: Our goal was to classify the reconstructed firing fields of recorded units as grid-like or not grid-like.
evidence: This describes the objective of the statistical analysis.

claim: Two measures of firing behavior suitable for classification were identified.
source: In a first step, we identified two measures of firing behavior that were suitable for this classification.
evidence: This describes the first step of the statistical analysis approach.

claim: The joint distribution of measures was estimated when the generating cell is either a noisy grid cell, a cell with a noisy homogeneous firing field or a noisy place field like cell.
source: In a second step, we estimated the joint distribution of these measures when the generating cell is either a noisy grid cell, a cell with a noisy homogeneous firing field or a noisy place field like cell.
evidence: This describes the second step of the statistical analysis approach.

claim: The rate function has a temporal resolution of 120 Hz.
source: The rate function has a temporal resolution of 120 Hz.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the simulation.

claim: 5000 grid cell units were simulated for each of nine different βsignal values.
source: We simulated 5000 grid cell units for each of nine different βsignal values (i2 for evenly spaced i between 0.18 and 1).
evidence: This describes the simulation parameters.

claim: All firing fields that had less than three peaks in the area covered by the trajectory were discarded.
source: We discarded all firing fields that had less than three peaks in the area covered by the trajectory; these are a priori not recognizable as grid-like.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion for simulated cells.

claim: 27,450 units whose firing rate was determined by a grid-like firing field were generated.
source: This resulted in 27,450 units whose firing rate was determined by a grid-like firing field.
evidence: This reports the number of simulated grid cells.

claim: 37,500 simulated units whose firing fields ranged from completely uniform to spatially structured fields were generated.
source: This resulted in 37,500 simulated units whose firing fields ranged from completely uniform (βsignal = 0) to spatially structured fields (βsignal > 0).
evidence: This reports the number of simulated non-grid cells.

claim: Computation of the gridness score is analogous to Langston et al., 2010 and Brandon et al., 2011.
source: Computation of the gridness score is analogous to (Langston et al., 2010; Brandon et al., 2011).
evidence: This references the method used for computing gridness scores.

claim: The gridness measure is sensitive to how the ellipse is fit in the 2D autocorrelation.
source: Brandon et al. (2011) noted that this measure is sensitive to how the ellipse is fit in the 2D autocorrelation.
evidence: This references a known limitation of the gridness measure.

claim: A two-step procedure was used to fit an ellipse.
source: We used a two-step procedure to fit an ellipse.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach for ellipse fitting.

claim: The set of candidate ellipses was constrained to those that passed through at least one non-central peak in the 2D autocorrelation.
source: We constrained the set of candidate ellipses to those that passed through at least one non-central peak in the 2D autocorrelation.
evidence: This describes a constraint in the ellipse fitting procedure.

claim: The RMSE between all ellipse predictions and the 2D autocorrelation functions was computed.
source: To this end, we computed the RMSE (root-mean-square error) between all ellipse predictions and the 2D autocorrelation functions.
evidence: This describes a step in the ellipse selection process.

claim: A minimum shift algorithm was used to select ellipses that captured six peaks and valleys in the autocorrelation function.
source: We then used a minimum shift algorithm to select ellipses that captured six peaks and valleys in the autocorrelation function better than ellipses in the local neighborhood of possible ellipses (the window of the minimum shift algorithm is N/5).
evidence: This describes the algorithm used for ellipse selection.

claim: The final gridness score was the maximum of the gridness scores computed for the selected ellipses.
source: The final gridness score was then the maximum of the gridness scores computed for these ellipses.
evidence: This describes how the final gridness score was determined.

claim: ROC curves were computed to evaluate the power of the gridscore implementation to separate grid cells from non-grid cells.
source: To evaluate the power of the gridscore implementation to separate grid cells from non-grid cells, we computed gridness scores for all simulated units with grid-like firing fields. We then compared how well the gridscore separated units with firing rates determined by noise (βsignal = 0) from those whose firing rate was at least partly determined by the grid firing field (βsignal >0). To this end, we computed ROC curves and used the area under the curve as a measure of discriminatory power.
evidence: This describes the validation method for the gridness score.

claim: The probabilities Pgrid and Pnongrid were computed from the simulation results with grid-like, place field-like and homogeneous firing fields.
source: The probabilities Pgrid and Pnongrid were computed from the simulation results with grid-like, place field-like and homogeneous firing fields.
evidence: This describes how the likelihood estimates were derived.

claim: A Kernel density estimate was used to locally pool simulated gridness scores and ffm indices to compute the likelihood.
source: Since the gridness score and ffm index are continuous values, we locally pool simulated gridness scores and ffm indices to compute the likelihood. This pooling is carried out by a Kernel density estimate and the bandwidth (size of pooling) is determined via 10-fold cross validation.
evidence: This describes the statistical method for likelihood estimation.

claim: A logit transformation was applied to avoid boundary artifacts.
source: Since the gridness score and firing field modulation measures are bounded, we applied a logit transformation to avoid boundary artifacts.
evidence: This describes a data transformation step.

claim: Only units with βsignal > 0.15 were considered as simulations of grid cells for the grid density estimate.
source: We only considered units with βsignal > 0.15 as simulations of grid cells for the grid density estimate.
evidence: This describes a criterion for including simulated cells in the analysis.

claim: Removing units with βsignal < 0.15 for the density estimation makes the estimates more conservative.
source: Removing these units for the density estimation therefore makes our estimates more conservative.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the effect of the exclusion criterion.

claim: The log likelihood approach performed better than only using the gridness score for all noise levels.
source: The log likelihood approach performed better than only using the gridness score for all noise levels.
evidence: This reports a comparison of analysis methods, with reference to Methods Figure 5B.
